newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Rabin assassin studies Bible alone in cell.
newsitem.headline: Rabin assassin studies Bible alone in cell.

text.p: Yigal Amir, the religious Jew who assassinated Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin nearly a year ago, spends most of his days and nights studying the Bible and other Jewish texts alone in his cell.

His family says Amir, sentenced to life in prison for murdering Rabin and injuring his bodyguard, is the sole inmate in a section of Beersheba prison refurbished especially for him. Prison officials have kept him in solitary confinement.
"He's alone 24 hours a day. He spends all his time studying the Bible. He said he's sleeping just four hours a night and studying the rest of the time," said Amir's mother Geula.
Amir, 26, who was in his third year of law school before the murder, spends an hour a day alone in the prison courtyard and eats his meals in his four-square-metre (yard) cell.
Geula Amir told Reuters there were 11 closed-circuit television cameras in and around the cell including one in the bathroom.

Amir is allowed to phone home twice a week and is eligible for a 30-minute visit with his family in prison once a week but the visits have been suspended since August as punishment for his covering one of the cameras with a piece of cloth.

Amir staged a two-week hunger strike in protest over prison conditions, demanding he be allowed more religious books and a fan in his cell. He also complained that prison officials had confiscated letters he wrote.
"It got to be so hot without a fan in his cell that he reversed his schedule. He would sleep during the day and study at night," Geula Amir said.
Prison officials say Amir is being treated like any other inmate.

The family has asked the Association of Civil Rights in Israel, which has had Islamic Hamas militants among its clients, to lobby the Prison Authority on behalf of Amir and his brother Hagai, sentenced to 12 years for helping Yigal plot the murder.
Family members hope the brothers will eventually be allowed to serve out their sentences in one cell. Any parole for Yigal Amir would require a presidential decision.
The family denied reports Yigal Amir was writing a book about the assassination and said he was not looking for a bride.
"He could easily have a bride if he wanted one. Many women have expressed interest. Not just any women but quality women," said Amir's father Shlomo.
